description: Rate control — the encoder system that adjusts QP per frame/region to hit a target bitrate or quality — decomposed. Real-time, streaming, and VOD scenarios each have different rate-control requirements. The 5 main modes (CBR, VBR, CRF, capped CRF, ABR) trade quality consistency against bitrate predictability. Each operates by adjusting per-frame QP based on a feedback model from buffer state and complexity estimation.

sub_mechanisms.name: CRF_constant_rate_factor
sub_mechanisms.definition: Targets constant perceived quality: QP varies per frame so that visual quality stays roughly constant. The rate factor (a scalar 0-51) sets the quality target; bitrate varies with content complexity.
sub_mechanisms.why: What viewers actually want: consistent quality. Simple content uses few bits; complex content uses many. CRF is the default mode for x264/x265 because it produces the best quality-per-bit on average.

sub_mechanisms.name: VBR_variable_bitrate
sub_mechanisms.definition: Targets an average bitrate over the whole video; QP and per-frame bitrate vary widely to hit the average.
sub_mechanisms.why: Good middle ground: target storage size while preserving quality consistency. Used for VOD downloads where the file size matters but per-frame bitrate doesn't.

sub_mechanisms.name: CBR_constant_bitrate
sub_mechanisms.definition: Targets a strict bitrate every frame (within a small window). QP varies to maintain bitrate; quality varies as content changes.
sub_mechanisms.why: Required for live streaming and broadcast where network bandwidth is fixed. Quality dips on complex scenes are accepted because the alternative (buffer underrun) is worse.

sub_mechanisms.name: capped_CRF
sub_mechanisms.definition: CRF with a maximum bitrate cap. Quality stays constant (CRF mode) until bitrate hits the cap; then it caps and quality may drop on the hardest scenes.
sub_mechanisms.why: Compromise between CRF (quality consistent) and VBR (bitrate predictable). Common for streaming where bandwidth is variable but bounded — the cap prevents buffer overflow.

sub_mechanisms.name: ABR_average_bitrate
sub_mechanisms.definition: Targets a specific average bitrate exactly, with the encoder doing 2-pass analysis (first pass measures complexity, second pass distributes bits).
sub_mechanisms.why: Used when target file size is critical (e.g., specific ABR ladder rung). 2-pass mode produces better quality at the target bitrate than 1-pass because the encoder knows the full complexity distribution before encoding.

sub_mechanisms.name: two_pass_analysis
sub_mechanisms.definition: First pass: encode at constant QP, measure per-frame bit cost. Second pass: redistribute bits per frame based on the first-pass measurements, achieving the target bitrate with better quality.
sub_mechanisms.why: Single-pass rate control guesses future complexity; two-pass knows it. Two-pass beats single-pass at the same bitrate by 5-15% PSNR. Cost is encoding the stream twice.

sub_mechanisms.name: vbv_buffer_model
sub_mechanisms.definition: Video Buffer Verifier: a model of a hypothetical receiver buffer with fixed size and constant fill rate. The encoder must not overflow or underflow this buffer.
sub_mechanisms.why: Standardised buffer model lets encoders produce streams that work on any decoder. Encoders constrain per-frame bit cost so the VBV stays within bounds. The VBV is the standard's way of ensuring decode feasibility.

sub_mechanisms.name: macroblock_tree_complexity
sub_mechanisms.definition: x264's 'MB-tree' algorithm: estimates which macroblocks will be referenced by future frames and allocates more bits to those (so future frames have better predictors).
sub_mechanisms.why: Bits spent on a reference frame's high-quality macroblocks pay off across all future frames that use them as prediction. MB-tree allocates bits to the most-used reference macroblocks, improving overall efficiency by ~5-10%.

sub_mechanisms.name: psycho_visual_rate_control
sub_mechanisms.definition: Adjusts per-region QP based on perceptual saliency: faces get more bits, background gets fewer; high-contrast edges get more, smooth regions get less.
sub_mechanisms.why: Bit budget allocated by perceptual importance. PSNR-tuned RC over-spends bits on smooth regions (low MSE per bit), under-spends on faces. PSY-RC corrects this; gains ~10% subjective quality at the same bitrate.

sub_mechanisms.name: adaptive_quantisation
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-block QP variation derived from local complexity (variance, mode, edge strength). High-complexity blocks get finer QP; flat blocks get coarser.
sub_mechanisms.why: Same total bit budget allocated where it matters most. Adaptive Q (called AQ in x264) is a per-frame application of MB-tree's logic — extracts ~5-10% subjective quality.

sub_mechanisms.name: look_ahead_buffer
sub_mechanisms.definition: Encoder maintains a buffer of N future frames to analyse before encoding the current frame. Used for B-frame placement, scene change detection, and RC decisions.
sub_mechanisms.why: Future knowledge improves current decisions. Scene change before a high-QP frame means that frame is a good IDR candidate; complex future frames mean the current one should leave bits available. Look-ahead is one of x264's defining quality features.

sub_mechanisms.name: scene_change_detection
sub_mechanisms.definition: Frame-to-frame complexity comparison: large jumps in inter-prediction residual cost indicate a scene change. Triggers IDR insertion + RC reset.
sub_mechanisms.why: Scene changes break inter-prediction; encoding the new scene as a P-frame would waste many bits on the impossible prediction. IDR insertion at scene boundaries trades the I-frame cost for predictable future encoding.

derivation_rules.name: crf_quality_consistent_bitrate_varies
if: the goal is consistent perceived quality
then: CRF rate control beats CBR for average-quality optimisation
derivation_rules.why: CRF allocates bits where they're needed. Simple frames use few; complex frames use many. CBR forces equal bits per frame, wasting them on simple frames and starving complex ones.

derivation_rules.name: two_pass_beats_single_pass_at_known_bitrate
if: the target is a specific average bitrate
then: two-pass beats single-pass by 5-15% quality at that bitrate
derivation_rules.why: Single-pass must guess future complexity; two-pass knows it. Optimal bit allocation requires knowing the whole complexity distribution. Cost is 2x encode time.

derivation_rules.name: mb_tree_amortises_bits_across_dependencies
if: a macroblock will be referenced by many future frames
then: allocating more bits to it improves all those future frames
derivation_rules.why: Reference quality propagates: high-quality reference → high-quality prediction → low residual → fewer bits future. MB-tree's analysis identifies these high-impact macroblocks; allocating extra bits there has compounding gains.

derivation_rules.name: psy_rc_matches_hvs_attention
if: bits are allocated by perceptual saliency
then: subjective quality improves at the same average bitrate
derivation_rules.why: PSNR-tuned RC over-spends on the wrong regions. PSY-RC's saliency model (faces, edges, motion) gets bits where viewers notice them. The same bitrate, allocated better, scores higher on subjective tests.

derivation_rules.name: vbv_buffer_constraint_ensures_decode_feasibility
if: a stream meets the VBV buffer model constraints
then: all conformant decoders can decode it without buffer underrun
derivation_rules.why: VBV is the standard's contract: encoders that respect it produce universally-decodable streams. Per-frame bit budget is constrained to keep the hypothetical buffer in bounds — without this, encoders could create streams that exceed decoder memory.
